author: Shareholders Unite
title: When Will The Rot Stop?
text:
Waiting for Cramer's 10 points to be fulfilled to signal the end of the market selloff, or jump in now? We develop some ideas below.
The market selloff is reaching worrying proportions. Now that the erstwhile FANGs are also rolling over, nothing seems to be on firm ground anymore, apart perhaps from a few really defensive stocks.
Market observer Jim Cramer has posted a handy 10 point list of conditions that need to be met before stocks can rebound and the worst is over. In short summary:
Selling of Apple ( AAPL ) needs to stop, and this is likely after another few downgrades. Facebook ( FB ) needs to appoint an adult as the stock has become toxic. Software stocks have to stop falling as there is nothing fundamentally wrong with them. There isn't enough buying the dip yet; we have further to fall. We need a resolution to the China trade war. There are fears the US administration would be quite happy cutting China off entirely to stop its progress, that's bad for business. Fed needs to moderate its stance on rate hikes. There is confusion as a recession doesn't look to be on the horizon. Technically, the market chart still look ugly. Retail can't handle rate hikes, which is why they're going down. We're not in oversold conditions yet. We think these are valid points, but you could be waiting forever before you saw them all transpire. We also think that Cramer is overlooking what is a more fundamental difference in views: is this is just a substantial correction, or is the stock market telling us that economic conditions are taking a serious turn for the worse and that we're entering a bear market?
We think this is the main reason there is less "buy the dip" activity now than in previous years. Investors fear a slowdown in growth and are worried that Q3 earnings are as good as they will get.
So we see the main risks as follows, most of which are related to the health of the world economy:
China World economic slowdown Eurozone As long as we don't have more serious economic problems, like a substantial decline of economic growth or a renewed flare-up of the eurozone crisis, stocks will find a bottom sooner rather than later. There has been a really substantial amount of selling (especially in tech names) already and more reasonable valuations have emerged.
We also note that shares are not the only asset class that are falling on the expectations of a worsening economic outlook. What to think of the sudden and substantial crash (there really isn't another word for that) in oil?
It's a little curious that Cramer didn't mention oil, because this is quite a decline. We realize that it is in part a reaction to the exemptions that the US administration gave to some importers of Iranian oil, but not even talk of OPEC (or, more immediately, Saudi) production cuts has managed to arrest this. It's clearly also driven by fears of a slowing world economy.
China We entirely agree with Cramer on his fifth point about China. The fears that the US administration seems to want to stop Chinese technological evolution in its tracks (or at least slow it down considerably) are warranted.
While the president fulminates about the bilateral trade deficit with China, this is fairly meaningless for a number of reasons:
Much of the value added is produced elsewhere, most notably the US. A bilateral deficit isn't amenable to meaningful solutions. Reducing the one with China will simply increase deficits with other countries as long as the US refrains from changing its savings deficit. China's trade surplus has all but disappeared. It's much harder to argue that they are big trade violators today than it was five or 10 years ago. In general, this ignores the progress China has made on trade and intellectual property and currency management. Trade isn't a zero-sum game. What seems to be in the crosshairs of the administration is the China 2025 program. China 2025 comprises of a series of measures to increase China's role in 10 different high-tech industries: information technology, high-end machinery and robotics, aerospace, marine equipment and ships, advanced rail transport, new-energy vehicles, electric power, agricultural machinery, new materials, and bio-medical.
Although this is simply a fairly standard industrial policy initiative which many other countries embark upon (including the US), coming from China it hasn't been well received in certain corners of the administration. Here is Peter Navarro (from Bloomberg ):
China in my view brazenly has released this China 2025 plan that basically told the rest of the world, 'We’re going to dominate every single emerging industry of the future, and therefore your economies aren’t going to have a future'.
This is largely hyperbole, of course. China developing high-tech industries doesn't prevent other countries from doing the same.
Instead of trying to prevent China from accelerating its high-tech industries and risking a world recession in the process, the US could embark on something similar.
We have argued that the public sector has, in the not-so-distant past, financed a host fundamental research from which a surprisingly large proportion of today's innovations have come from.
This kind of fundamental research produces stunning returns, although they take years, more likely decades, to materialize.
The risk that the US is, in the name of trade complaints, trying to stifle Chinese economic development, is a serious one. In following companies this quarter, we've come across quite a large number of cases in which management argued that they were moving their sourcing or production out of China as a result of the US tariffs.
These moves are actually boosting the US, though. From CNN (our emphasis):
US tariffs are prompting companies to move some production out of China, but it's not going where President Donald Trump would prefer . The trade war has made more than $250 billion of Chinese exports more expensive for Americans — from leather belts to refrigerators to motorcycles. The disruption to the world's biggest trading relationship has electronics manufacturers, industrial machinery makers and fashion brands working on shifting some of their assembly lines. "We are flooded by inquiries," said William Ma, group managing director of Kerry Logistics, a Hong Kong-based firm that helps companies around the world manage their supply chains. "It all happens after the trade war." Many firms are keeping much of their operations in China, which offers a giant domestic market and advantages that businesses struggle to find elsewhere. But those that are moving aren't flocking to the United States. Instead, they're looking to transfer work to other Asian countries .
And this risks slowly causing the Chinese economy to keel over - something that won't go unnoticed for investors in US markets. Actually we think this is already in part responsible for the selloff.
China is, after all, the second-biggest economy in the world. A significant Chinese slowdown (let alone a hard landing) will have repercussions for the world economy at large. In particular:
It will add slower growth as a headache to many emerging economies, on top of a rising dollar and US monetary tightening. Slow growth is the last thing that Italy's public finances need, as they haven't been able to get the debt/GDP ratio down during the years of growth, super low interest rates, and bond buying by the ECB (which is set to expire next month). There is a surprising upside to this. The US has been aggressive with China because the administration assumes that the trade conflict hurts China much more than it hurts the US. Trump himself often pointed out the decline in the Chinese stock market as evidence of that.
But now that US markets are also misbehaving, it perhaps shows the US government that there is a downside to their strategy as well. Whether that is enough to dial back the trade war remains to be seen, though.
We're not going to repeat our Italy fears here, but that situation is extremely risky. Growth has already disappeared entirely. Italian banks are already suffering from mark to market on their large bond portfolios. The ECB is going to end bond purchases next month. It has been the only net buyer of Italian bonds in the past three years.
We have explained how these issues can start feeding on themselves and spin out of control pretty rapidly (this happened earlier in 2012 until ECB President Draghi invoked his "whatever it takes").
To add to these problems, there is a new populist government that is going to embark on a rather epic spending spree, at the worst possible time. The only figure one has to watch is this (from Bloomberg ):
We fear that 4% yield might be a threshold for things getting considerably worse.
Sentiment There is actually another danger now that markets like oil and shares are falling so rapidly. These falls could easily scare and/or force investors into additional selling, that is, snowballing into something bigger.
As it gets bigger, there will come a moment when it starts influencing the real economy through that intangible called 'sentiment,' and the distinctly more tangible 'wealth effect.'
We're not sure we are close to that (which basically is anybody's guess), but this is a scenario that isn't far-fetched. After the euphoria of the past year or so, sentiment has turned quite a bit.
Conclusion While Cramer's 10 criteria for a market bottom are quite sound, we feel they are two market-centric. We think the real question is whether this is a correction or the beginning of a bear market.
And the answer to that doesn't lie in the stock market, but in the world economy (especially as it pertains to events in China and Italy). To make matters worse, a continuous market selloff itself can start to exert a negative effect on the economy at some stage.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
